claim: Small conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK channels) are present in spines.
source: Small conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK channels) are present in spines and can be activated by backpropagating action potentials (APs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact.

claim: SK channels can be activated by backpropagating action potentials (APs).
source: Small conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK channels) are present in spines and can be activated by backpropagating action potentials (APs).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: EPSPs in cortical pyramidal neurons were suppressed by preceding APs in an SK-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with this idea, EPSPs in both cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons were suppressed by preceding APs in an SK-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: EPSPs in hippocampal pyramidal neurons were suppressed by preceding APs in an SK-dependent manner.
source: Consistent with this idea, EPSPs in both cortical and hippocampal pyramidal neurons were suppressed by preceding APs in an SK-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs in cortical pyramidal neurons depended on their precise timing.
source: In cortical pyramidal neurons EPSP suppression by preceding APs depended on their precise timing as well as the distance of activated synapses from the soma, was dendritic in origin, and involved SK-dependent suppression of NMDA receptor activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1d-e showing timing-dependent effects.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs in cortical pyramidal neurons depended on the distance of activated synapses from the soma.
source: In cortical pyramidal neurons EPSP suppression by preceding APs depended on their precise timing as well as the distance of activated synapses from the soma, was dendritic in origin, and involved SK-dependent suppression of NMDA receptor activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1g showing correlation with EPSP rise time.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs in cortical pyramidal neurons was dendritic in origin.
source: In cortical pyramidal neurons EPSP suppression by preceding APs depended on their precise timing as well as the distance of activated synapses from the soma, was dendritic in origin, and involved SK-dependent suppression of NMDA receptor activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing minimal somatic contribution.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs involved SK-dependent suppression of NMDA receptor activation.
source: In cortical pyramidal neurons EPSP suppression by preceding APs depended on their precise timing as well as the distance of activated synapses from the soma, was dendritic in origin, and involved SK-dependent suppression of NMDA receptor activation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing NMDAR dependence.

claim: SK channel activation by backpropagating APs gated STDP induction during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing.
source: As a result SK channel activation by backpropagating APs gated STDP induction during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing, with both LTP and LTD absent under control conditions but present after SK channel block.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Both LTP and LTD were absent under control conditions during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing.
source: As a result SK channel activation by backpropagating APs gated STDP induction during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing, with both LTP and LTD absent under control conditions but present after SK channel block.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7a-d.

claim: Both LTP and LTD were present after SK channel block during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing.
source: As a result SK channel activation by backpropagating APs gated STDP induction during low-frequency AP-EPSP pairing, with both LTP and LTD absent under control conditions but present after SK channel block.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 7a-d.

claim: SK channels in spines regulate the amplitude of EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus.
source: Small conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK channels) in spines regulate the amplitude of EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus and amygdala (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Faber et al., 2005; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SK channels in spines regulate the amplitude of EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the amygdala.
source: Small conductance calcium-activated potassium channels (SK channels) in spines regulate the amplitude of EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus and amygdala (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Faber et al., 2005; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Calcium influx into spines during EPSPs leads to SK channel activation.
source: This earlier work has shown that calcium influx into spines during EPSPs leads to SK channel activation, which acts to reduce NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activation presumably by promoting voltage-dependent magnesium block (Mayer et al., 1984; Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SK channel activation acts to reduce NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activation by promoting voltage-dependent magnesium block.
source: This earlier work has shown that calcium influx into spines during EPSPs leads to SK channel activation, which acts to reduce NMDA receptor (NMDAR) activation presumably by promoting voltage-dependent magnesium block (Mayer et al., 1984; Nowak et al., 1984).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and the word 'presumably' indicates inference.

claim: SK channels in spines form a negative feedback loop controlling EPSP amplitude and calcium influx during EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus and amygdala.
source: These studies indicate that during EPSPs in pyramidal neurons in the hippocampus and amygdala SK channels in spines form a negative feedback loop controlling EPSP amplitude and calcium influx (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Faber et al., 2005; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SK channels in spines act to limit calcium influx into spines and dendrites during backpropagating APs in cortical pyramidal neurons.
source: In addition to their impact on EPSPs, we recently showed in cortical pyramidal neurons that SK channels in spines also act to limit calcium influx into spines and dendrites during backpropagating APs (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: NMDAR activation and calcium play a central role in synaptic plasticity.
source: Given the central role of NMDAR activation and calcium in synaptic plasticity (Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Yang et al., 1999), the capacity of SK channels to influence NMDAR activation and calcium influx into spines during EPSPs and APs is likely to have consequences on the induction of synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Blocking SK channel activation can promote and enhance long-term potentiation (LTP) evoked by tetanic stimulation in pyramidal neurons from the hippocampus.
source: Consistent with this idea, blocking SK channel activation, and thereby the impact of SK channels on NMDAR function, can promote and enhance long-term potentiation (LTP) evoked by tetanic stimulation in pyramidal neurons from the hippocampus (Behnisch and Reymann, 1998; Stackman et al., 2002) and amygdala (Faber et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Blocking SK channel activation can promote and enhance long-term potentiation (LTP) evoked by tetanic stimulation in pyramidal neurons from the amygdala.
source: Consistent with this idea, blocking SK channel activation, and thereby the impact of SK channels on NMDAR function, can promote and enhance long-term potentiation (LTP) evoked by tetanic stimulation in pyramidal neurons from the hippocampus (Behnisch and Reymann, 1998; Stackman et al., 2002) and amygdala (Faber et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of SK channels from spines contributes to LTP expression in hippocampal pyramidal neurons.
source: Loss of SK channels from spines has also been shown to contribute to LTP expression in hippocampal pyramidal neurons (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: mGluR activation facilitates LTP induction during STDP in hippocampal neurons via inhibition of SK channels.
source: Finally, a recent study observed that mGluR activation facilitates LTP induction during STDP in hippocampal neurons via inhibition of SK channels (Tigaret et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Generation of single APs 10 ms before EPSPs suppressed EPSP peak by approximately 30%.
source: Generation of single APs 10 ms before EPSPs (−10 ms timing) suppressed EPSP peak by approximately 30% (Figure 1b,c; n = 6).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1b,c.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs was significantly reduced by bath application of the SK channel blocker apamin.
source: This EPSP suppression was significantly reduced by bath application of the SK channel blocker apamin, indicating a role of SK channels (Figure 1b,c).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1b,c.

claim: The magnitude of SK-dependent EPSP suppression was dependent on the precise timing of EPSPs and postsynaptic APs.
source: The magnitude of SK-dependent EPSP suppression was dependent on the precise timing of EPSPs and postsynaptic APs, with EPSP suppression only observed when postsynaptic APs were evoked within a brief time window before EPSP onset (Figure 1d,e; n = 6).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1d,e.

claim: EPSP width was reduced by preceding postsynaptic APs in a time and SK-dependent manner.
source: EPSP width was also reduced by preceding postsynaptic APs in a time and SK-dependent manner (Figure 1f).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1f.

claim: EPSP suppression by preceding APs was not totally abolished by bath applications of apamin.
source: EPSP suppression by preceding APs was not totally abolished by bath applications of apamin (Figure 1e), indicating that in addition to SK channels other postsynaptic conductances activated by APs contribute to suppression of subsequently evoked EPSPs.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1e.

claim: In addition to SK channels, other postsynaptic conductances activated by APs contribute to suppression of subsequently evoked EPSPs.
source: EPSP suppression by preceding APs was not totally abolished by bath applications of apamin (Figure 1e), indicating that in addition to SK channels other postsynaptic conductances activated by APs contribute to suppression of subsequently evoked EPSPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete block by apamin shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Calcium influx into dendritic spines during backpropagating APs is regulated by SK channels in basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Previous findings in basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons indicate that calcium influx into dendritic spines during backpropagating APs is regulated by SK channels, with the impact of SK channels on spine calcium influx greater for spines located further from the soma (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The impact of SK channels on spine calcium influx is greater for spines located further from the soma in basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Previous findings in basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons indicate that calcium influx into dendritic spines during backpropagating APs is regulated by SK channels, with the impact of SK channels on spine calcium influx greater for spines located further from the soma (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Somatic EPSP rise time is positively correlated with the distance of active synapses from the soma of layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Previous work indicates that somatic EPSP rise time is positively correlated with the distance of active synapses from the soma of layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Letzkus et al., 2006), as expected due to dendritic filtering (Jack et al., 1971).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synaptic connections between layer 5 pyramidal neurons are made between 80 and 585 µm from the soma.
source: The range of EPSP rise times in our experiments was similar to that observed in a previous study using paired recordings from layer 5 pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex (Markram et al., 1997a), with this earlier work finding that synaptic connections between layer 5 pyramidal neurons are made between 80 and 585 µm from the soma (mean: 147 µm; median: 105 µm), with the majority of inputs on basal dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The majority of synaptic inputs between layer 5 pyramidal neurons are on basal dendrites.
source: The range of EPSP rise times in our experiments was similar to that observed in a previous study using paired recordings from layer 5 pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex (Markram et al., 1997a), with this earlier work finding that synaptic connections between layer 5 pyramidal neurons are made between 80 and 585 µm from the soma (mean: 147 µm; median: 105 µm), with the majority of inputs on basal dendrites.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The impact of SK channel block on EPSP suppression by preceding APs was positively correlated with EPSP rise-time.
source: Consistent with our earlier study showing that the impact of SK channels on calcium influx during backpropagating APs is greater at more distal dendritic locations, we found that the impact of SK channel block on EPSP suppression by preceding APs (−10 ms timing) was positively correlated with EPSP rise-time (Figure 1g; n = 16).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 1g.

claim: SK channels activated by backpropagating APs lead to greater suppression of EPSPs when they are generated at more distal dendritic locations.
source: These data suggest that SK channels activated by backpropagating APs lead to greater suppression of EPSPs when they are generated at more distal dendritic locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between EPSP rise time and SK channel impact shown in Figure 1g.

claim: Preceding postsynaptic APs suppressed EPSPs in cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons in an SK-dependent manner.
source: These experiments indicated that preceding postsynaptic APs suppressed EPSPs in both cortical layer 2/3 and hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons in an SK-dependent manner (Figure 2a-d), as observed in layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2a-d.

claim: Blocking SK channels had no impact on the amplitude of EPSPs alone in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, these experiments also revealed that blocking SK channels had no impact on the amplitude of EPSPs alone in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2e), while it increased the amplitude of EPSPs evoked on their own in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2f), as observed by others (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2e.

claim: Blocking SK channels increased the amplitude of EPSPs evoked on their own in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Interestingly, these experiments also revealed that blocking SK channels had no impact on the amplitude of EPSPs alone in layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2e), while it increased the amplitude of EPSPs evoked on their own in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Figure 2f), as observed by others (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2f and citations to previous work.

claim: Blocking SK channels had no impact on unitary EPSPs in layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Blocking SK channels also had no impact on unitary EPSPs in layer 5 pyramidal neurons (see Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data in Figure 1c.

claim: In contrast to CA1 pyramidal neurons, calcium influx via NMDARs is not sufficient to activate SK channels in cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: These observations suggest that, in contrast to CA1 pyramidal neurons (Wang et al., 2014), calcium influx via NMDARs is not sufficient to activate SK channels in cortical layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal neurons, and that this requires AP generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of SK channel block on EPSPs alone in different cell types.

claim: In contrast to CA1 pyramidal neurons, calcium influx via NMDARs is not sufficient to activate SK channels in cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: These observations suggest that, in contrast to CA1 pyramidal neurons (Wang et al., 2014), calcium influx via NMDARs is not sufficient to activate SK channels in cortical layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal neurons, and that this requires AP generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of SK channel block on EPSPs alone in different cell types.

claim: SK channel activation in cortical layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal neurons requires AP generation.
source: These observations suggest that, in contrast to CA1 pyramidal neurons (Wang et al., 2014), calcium influx via NMDARs is not sufficient to activate SK channels in cortical layer 2/3 and layer 5 pyramidal neurons, and that this requires AP generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SK channels affect EPSPs only when paired with APs.

claim: The extent of AP-induced suppression of aEPSP peak was much smaller than that observed during unitary EPSPs.
source: Preceding APs suppressed aEPSPs during pairing at −10 ms, however, the extent of AP-induced suppression of aEPSP peak was much smaller than that observed during unitary EPSPs and was insensitive to apamin (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3a,b.

claim: AP-induced suppression of aEPSP peak was insensitive to apamin.
source: Preceding APs suppressed aEPSPs during pairing at −10 ms, however, the extent of AP-induced suppression of aEPSP peak was much smaller than that observed during unitary EPSPs and was insensitive to apamin (Figure 3a,b).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3a,b.

claim: An effect of apamin on AP-induced suppression of aEPSP half-width was observed, although this effect was small.
source: An effect of apamin on AP-induced suppression of aEPSP half-width was observed, although this effect was small (Figure 3c; n = 7).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3c.

claim: Somatic SK channels activated by APs have little impact on EPSP peak.
source: These data suggest that somatic SK channels activated by APs have little impact on EPSP peak, supporting the idea that AP-induced suppression of unitary EPSPs is primarily due to dendritic SK channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the aEPSP experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: AP-induced suppression of unitary EPSPs is primarily due to dendritic SK channels.
source: These data suggest that somatic SK channels activated by APs have little impact on EPSP peak, supporting the idea that AP-induced suppression of unitary EPSPs is primarily due to dendritic SK channels.
evidence: This is inferred from the aEPSP experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Low concentrations of BAPTA (300 μM) block somatic SK channels in layer 5 pyramidal neurons while preserving the function of SK channels in dendrites.
source: We have recently shown that this blocks somatic SK channels in layer 5 pyramidal neurons, while preserving the function of SK channels in dendrites (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Low concentrations of BAPTA completely abolished the SK-mediated component of the somatic mAHP in layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Consistent with these earlier observations, low concentrations of BAPTA completely abolished the SK-mediated component of the somatic mAHP in layer 5 pyramidal neurons (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3d.

claim: Under conditions with intracellular BAPTA, preceding APs suppressed unitary EPSPs to a similar extent to that observed in the absence of BAPTA in an apamin-dependent manner.
source: Under these conditions preceding APs suppressed unitary EPSPs to a similar extent to that observed in the absence of BAPTA in an apamin-dependent manner (Figure 3e–h; n = 6; compare with Figure 1).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3e-h.

claim: Dendritic SK channels activated by backpropagating APs are responsible for suppression of subsequently evoked unitary EPSPs.
source: Together, these data provide strong support for the idea that dendritic SK channels activated by backpropagating APs are responsible for suppression of subsequently evoked unitary EPSPs.
evidence: This is inferred from the BAPTA experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: SK channels activated during EPSPs suppress NMDAR activation in some cell types.
source: While EPSPs evoked on their own were not affected by SK channel block in cortical pyramidal neurons (Figure 1c and Figure 2e), previous work in other cell types indicates that SK channels activated during EPSPs suppress NMDAR activation (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Faber et al., 2005; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Apamin had no impact on EPSP suppression by preceding APs in the presence of the NMDAR antagonist AP5.
source: Consistent with a critical role of NMDARs, apamin had no impact on EPSP suppression by preceding APs (−10 ms timing) in the presence of the NMDAR antagonist AP5 (Figure 4a–c; n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Blocking NMDARs with AP5 enhanced EPSP suppression by preceding APs.
source: Surprisingly, these experiments revealed that blocking NMDARs with AP5 enhanced EPSP suppression by preceding APs (Figure 4a–c; n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4a-c.

claim: Block of NMDARs with AP5 increased the impact of preceding APs on EPSP width.
source: Block of NMDARs with AP5 also increased the impact of preceding APs on EPSP width (Figure 4d; n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4d.

claim: In the presence of AP5, EPSP width was slightly increased by SK channel block.
source: In contrast to observations on EPSP peak, however, in the presence of AP5 EPSP width was slightly increased by SK channel block (Figure 4d; n = 5).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 4d.

claim: The small effect of SK channel block on EPSP width in the presence of AP5 is presumably due to block of somatic SK channels.
source: This small effect on EPSP width is presumably due to block of somatic SK channels, and resembles the impact of SK channel block on AP-induced suppression of somatic aEPSP width (see Figure 3c).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with aEPSP data in Figure 3c.

claim: Backpropagating APs enhance NMDAR activation, with the extent of NMDAR activation regulated by SK channels.
source: One interpretation of these observations is that backpropagating APs enhance NMDAR activation, with the extent of NMDAR activation regulated by SK channels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data from Figure 4.

claim: Blocking NMDARs both increases AP-induced EPSP suppression and occludes the impact of apamin.
source: As a result, blocking NMDARs both increases AP-induced EPSP suppression and occludes the impact of apamin.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The model reproduced SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs.
source: Using this model all aspects of the experimental data could be reproduced, including SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs (Figure 5b; compare with Figure 1b), as well as the observation that EPSP suppression was enhanced following NMDAR block (Figure 5b,c; compare with Figure 4a), and the finding that NMDAR block removed the dependence of EPSP suppression on SK channels (Figure 5c; compare with Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model reproduced the observation that EPSP suppression was enhanced following NMDAR block.
source: Using this model all aspects of the experimental data could be reproduced, including SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs (Figure 5b; compare with Figure 1b), as well as the observation that EPSP suppression was enhanced following NMDAR block (Figure 5b,c; compare with Figure 4a), and the finding that NMDAR block removed the dependence of EPSP suppression on SK channels (Figure 5c; compare with Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: The model reproduced the finding that NMDAR block removed the dependence of EPSP suppression on SK channels.
source: Using this model all aspects of the experimental data could be reproduced, including SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs (Figure 5b; compare with Figure 1b), as well as the observation that EPSP suppression was enhanced following NMDAR block (Figure 5b,c; compare with Figure 4a), and the finding that NMDAR block removed the dependence of EPSP suppression on SK channels (Figure 5c; compare with Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5.

claim: SK-dependent EPSP suppression in the model was dependent on AP-EPSP timing.
source: In addition, as observed experimentally, SK-dependent EPSP suppression in the model was dependent on AP-EPSP timing, with a timing of −10 ms suppressing EPSP peak by a similar amount to that seen experimentally (Figure 5d; compare with Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5d.

claim: SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs in the model decreased EPSP width.
source: SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs also decreased EPSP width (Figure 5e; compare with Figure 1f), and was greater for more distally generated EPSPs (Figure 5f; compare with Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5e.

claim: SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs in the model was greater for more distally generated EPSPs.
source: SK-dependent EPSP suppression by preceding APs also decreased EPSP width (Figure 5e; compare with Figure 1f), and was greater for more distally generated EPSPs (Figure 5f; compare with Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Switching off SK channels in spines increases backpropagating AP width, but not amplitude, with the greatest effect at distal dendritic locations.
source: These simulations indicated that switching off SK channels in spines increases backpropagating AP width, but not amplitude, with the greatest effect at distal dendritic locations (Figure 5g–i).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5g-i.

claim: The effect of SK channels on backpropagating APs leads to depolarisation of spine voltage as well as an increase in spine calcium influx through voltage-activated calcium channels.
source: This effect of SK channels leads to depolarisation of spine voltage as well as an increase in spine calcium influx through voltage-activated calcium channels (Figure 5j–l), which is greater for more distal spines and matches recent experimental observations (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 5j-l and supported by citation.

claim: SK channels in spines act to repolarize backpropagating APs and have a greater impact at more distal dendritic locations.
source: Together, these simulations suggest that SK channels in spines act to repolarize backpropagating APs and have a greater impact at more distal dendritic locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Activation of dendritic SK channels by backpropagating APs has minimal impact on somatic EPSPs.
source: As SK channels in the model were constrained to dendritic spines these simulations show that activation of dendritic SK channels by backpropagating APs has minimal impact on somatic EPSPs, supporting the conclusion from the aEPSP experiments that the impact of SK channels on unitary EPSPs is dendritic.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Preceding APs had opposing effects on current flow through AMPA and NMDA channels.
source: Preceding APs had opposing effects on current flow through AMPA and NMDA channels, leading to a decrease in AMPA current due to a reduction in driving force (Figure 6b), but an increase in NMDA current due to the impact of spine depolarisation during backpropagating APs on NMDA channel activation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6b,c.

claim: Preceding APs lead to a decrease in AMPA current due to a reduction in driving force.
source: Preceding APs had opposing effects on current flow through AMPA and NMDA channels, leading to a decrease in AMPA current due to a reduction in driving force (Figure 6b), but an increase in NMDA current due to the impact of spine depolarisation during backpropagating APs on NMDA channel activation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Preceding APs lead to an increase in NMDA current due to the impact of spine depolarisation during backpropagating APs on NMDA channel activation.
source: Preceding APs had opposing effects on current flow through AMPA and NMDA channels, leading to a decrease in AMPA current due to a reduction in driving force (Figure 6b), but an increase in NMDA current due to the impact of spine depolarisation during backpropagating APs on NMDA channel activation (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Switching SK channels off had minimal impact on AMPA current flow.
source: Switching SK channels off in these simulations had minimal impact on AMPA current flow (Figure 6b), but further increased NMDA current due to increased depolarisation of dendritic spines following broadening of backpropagating APs (Figure 6c; see Figure 5j).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Switching SK channels off further increased NMDA current due to increased depolarisation of dendritic spines following broadening of backpropagating APs.
source: Switching SK channels off in these simulations had minimal impact on AMPA current flow (Figure 6b), but further increased NMDA current due to increased depolarisation of dendritic spines following broadening of backpropagating APs (Figure 6c; see Figure 5j).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Preceding APs lead to EPSP suppression by reducing current flow through AMPA receptors, which is offset by NMDAR activation.
source: In conclusion, these stimulations indicate that preceding APs lead to EPSP suppression by reducing current flow through AMPA receptors, which is offset by NMDAR activation (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: Blocking SK channels reduces EPSP suppression, whereas blocking NMDARs increases EPSP suppression.
source: As the extent of NMDAR activation is controlled by SK channels, blocking SK channels reduces EPSP suppression, whereas blocking NMDARs increases EPSP suppression.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 6.

claim: When SK channels were restricted to active spines receiving synaptic input, turning SK channels off had essentially no impact on AP-induced EPSP suppression.
source: In simulations where SK channels were restricted to active spines receiving synaptic input (the vast minority), turning SK channels off had essentially no impact on AP-induced EPSP suppression (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6e.

claim: When SK channels were located in inactivated spines that did not receive synaptic input, blocking SK channels reduced EPSP suppression to a similar extent to that seen when SK channels were located in all spines.
source: In contrast, when SK channels were located in inactivated spines that did not receive synaptic input (the vast majority), blocking SK channels reduced EPSP suppression to a similar extent to that seen when SK channels were located in all spines (Figure 6f; compare with Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling shown in Figure 6f.

claim: SK-dependent suppression of EPSPs by APs is not due to the local impact of SK channels activated solely in spines receiving synaptic input, but requires global recruitment of SK channels along the entire length of the active basal dendrite.
source: These simulations indicate that SK-dependent suppression of EPSPs by APs is not due to the local impact of SK channels activated solely in spines receiving synaptic input, but requires global recruitment of SK channels along the entire length of the active basal dendrite.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 6e,f.

claim: The extent of NMDAR activation is crucial for determining the magnitude and sign of STDP.
source: As the extent of NMDAR activation is crucial for determining the magnitude and sign of STDP (Bi and Poo, 1998; Kampa et al., 2006; Markram et al., 1997b; Sjöström et al., 2001), activation of SK channels by backpropagating APs is likely to influence the induction of STDP during AP-EPSP pairing.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Low-frequency (0.2 Hz) single AP-EPSP pairing at both positive (+10 ms) and negative times (−10 ms) did not lead to STDP in layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source: Consistent with earlier work in layer 5 pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex (Kampa et al., 2006; Markram et al., 1997b), low-frequency (0.2 Hz) single AP-EPSP pairing at both positive (+10 ms) and negative times (−10 ms) did not lead to STDP (Figure 7a–d).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 7a-d and citations to previous work.

claim: Following block of SK channels with apamin, single AP pairing at −10 ms induced robust LTD.
source: In contrast, following block of SK channels with apamin single AP pairing at −10 ms induced robust LTD, whereas pairing at +10 ms induced robust LTP (Figure 7a–d; n = 6 and n = 5, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 7a-d.

claim: Following block of SK channels with apamin, single AP pairing at +10 ms induced robust LTP.
source: In contrast, following block of SK channels with apamin single AP pairing at −10 ms induced robust LTD, whereas pairing at +10 ms induced robust LTP (Figure 7a–d; n = 6 and n = 5, respectively).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 7a-d.

claim: Dendritic SK channels play a key role in regulating the induction of STDP in layer 5 pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex during single AP-EPSP pairing.
source: These data indicate that dendritic SK channels play a key role in regulating the induction of STDP in layer 5 pyramidal neurons in somatosensory cortex during single AP-EPSP pairing, presumably through their capacity to limit NMDAR activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the STDP experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: EPSPs with slower rise times underwent greater plasticity in the presence of apamin during pairing at both positive and negative times.
source: This analysis indicated that EPSPs with slower rise times, which are presumably generated at more distal locations, underwent greater plasticity in the presence of apamin during pairing at both positive and negative times (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 7e.

claim: APs evoked after EPSP onset shunt EPSPs at the soma of cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje neurons, reducing their amplitude.
source: APs evoked after EPSP onset have been shown to shunt EPSPs at the soma of cortical layer 5 pyramidal neurons and cerebellar Purkinje neurons, reducing their amplitude (Häusser et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Froemke et al. (2005) showed that preceding APs lead to EPSP suppression in cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
source: More relevant to our observations is the work by Froemke et al. (2005), who showed that preceding APs lead to EPSP suppression in cortical layer 2/3 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Froemke et al. (2005) attributed EPSP suppression to calcium-dependent NMDAR desensitisation.
source: In contrast to our findings, however, this study attributed EPSP suppression to calcium-dependent NMDAR desensitisation, due to its dependence on NMDAR activation and intracellular calcium (Froemke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The EPSP suppression described by Froemke et al. (2005) is likely to be mediated by the same SK-dependent mechanism described in this study.
source: Based on these observations, we predict that the EPSP suppression described by Froemke et al. (2005) is likely to be mediated by the same SK-dependent mechanism described here, rather than via calcium-dependent NMDAR desensitisation.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the current experimental findings.

claim: SK channels in hippocampal CA1 neurons can be activated by EPSPs alone, regulating NMDAR activation and EPSP amplitude.
source: Previous work indicates that SK channels in hippocampal CA1 neurons can be activated by EPSPs alone, regulating NMDAR activation and EPSP amplitude (Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007; Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Activation of SK channels in spines on basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal neurons during backpropagating APs is dependent on only R-type voltage-dependent calcium channels.
source: Activation of SK channels in spines on basal dendrites of layer 5 pyramidal during backpropagating APs has recently been shown to be dependent on only R-type voltage-dependent calcium channels (Jones and Stuart, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: SK channels in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons are thought to be activated by calcium influx through NMDARs.
source: In contrast, SK channels in hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons are thought to be activated by calcium influx through NMDARs (Ngo-Anh et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2014; although see Bloodgood and Sabatini, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Under control conditions, the extent of EPSP suppression due to reduced current flow through AMPA receptors is offset by increased NMDAR activation.
source: This increase in AP-induced EPSP suppression arises because under control conditions the extent of EPSP suppression due to reduced current flow through AMPA receptors is offset by increased NMDAR activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: Following NMDAR block, SK channels have little impact on EPSP suppression because SK channels predominately modulate NMDAR activation.
source: In addition, we observed that following NMDAR block SK channels had no impact on EPSP suppression. This is presumably the case as SK channels predominately modulate NMDAR activation, and have little impact on current flow through AMPA receptors (see Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and modeling data shown in Figures 4 and 6.

claim: Depolarisation of dendritic spines by backpropagating APs increases NMDAR activation due to relief of magnesium block.
source: Depolarisation of dendritic spines by backpropagating APs not surprisingly increases NMDAR activation due to relief of magnesium block (Kampa et al., 2006; Mayer et al., 1984; Nowak et al., 1984), while at the same time reduces current flow through AMPA receptors due to a reduction in electrochemical driving force.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Depolarisation of dendritic spines by backpropagating APs reduces current flow through AMPA receptors due to a reduction in electrochemical driving force.
source: Depolarisation of dendritic spines by backpropagating APs not surprisingly increases NMDAR activation due to relief of magnesium block (Kampa et al., 2006; Mayer et al., 1984; Nowak et al., 1984), while at the same time reduces current flow through AMPA receptors due to a reduction in electrochemical driving force.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling data and represents established biophysical principles.

claim: SK channels control spine voltage during backpropagating APs and thereby regulate the extent of NMDAR activation.
source: As SK channels control spine voltage during backpropagating APs they regulate the extent of NMDAR activation, which presumably also explains their capacity to gate STDP induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: The capacity of SK channels to regulate NMDAR activation explains their capacity to gate STDP induction.
source: As SK channels control spine voltage during backpropagating APs they regulate the extent of NMDAR activation, which presumably also explains their capacity to gate STDP induction.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: The impact of SK channel activation on backpropagating AP width and thereby spine depolarization is greater at more distal dendritic locations.
source: As a result the impact of SK channel activation on backpropagating AP width and thereby spine depolarization is greater at more distal dendritic locations.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results shown in Figure 5.

claim: The extent of AP-induced EPSP suppression was greater for more distal synaptic inputs.
source: This can explain why the extent of AP-induced EPSP suppression was greater for more distal synaptic inputs (Figure 1g), and may also explain the great impact of preceding APs on distal compared to proximal EPSPs in earlier work in layer 2/3 neurons (Froemke et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1g and citation to previous work.

claim: The absolute magnitude of STDP observed during AP-EPSP pairing at both positive and negative times was positively correlated with somatic EPSP rise time.
source: This dependence of EPSP suppression on synapse location also impacted on STDP, with the absolute magnitude of STDP observed during AP-EPSP pairing at both positive and negative times positively correlated with somatic EPSP rise time (Figure 7e).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 7e.

claim: STDP is a form of synaptic plasticity where the strength of synaptic connections is modified by the precise timing of synaptic input and postsynaptic APs.
source: STDP is a form of synaptic plasticity where the strength of synaptic connections is modified by the precise timing of synaptic input and postsynaptic APs (Bi and Poo, 1998; Markram et al., 1997b; Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and represents established knowledge.

claim: Unitary synaptic connections between layer 5 pyramidal neurons do not display LTP when EPSPs are paired with APs at positive timings (+10 ms) in both somatosensory and visual cortex.
source: For example, unitary synaptic connections between layer 5 pyramidal neurons do not display LTP when EPSPs are paired with APs at positive timings (+10 ms) in both somatosensory and visual cortex (Kampa and Stuart, 2006; Markram et al., 1997b; Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Low-frequency single AP pairing of unitary EPSPs between layer 5 pyramidal neurons does not produce LTD in somatosensory cortex.
source: Low-frequency single AP pairing of unitary EPSPs between layer 5 pyramidal neurons also does not produce LTD in somatosensory cortex (Kampa et al., 2006; Markram et al., 1997b), although this does lead to LTD in visual cortex (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Low-frequency single AP pairing of unitary EPSPs between layer 5 pyramidal neurons leads to LTD in visual cortex.
source: Low-frequency single AP pairing of unitary EPSPs between layer 5 pyramidal neurons also does not produce LTD in somatosensory cortex (Kampa et al., 2006; Markram et al., 1997b), although this does lead to LTD in visual cortex (Sjöström et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The input resistance of layer 5 pyramidal neurons is significantly higher in visual compared to somatosensory cortex.
source: The input resistance of layer 5 pyramidal neurons is significantly higher in visual compared to somatosensory cortex (Sjöström et al., 2001; Williams and Stuart, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The capacity of SK channels to gate the induction of STDP during low-frequency single AP-EPSP pairing provides a means to negate the impact of accidental or spurious AP-EPSP pairings on synaptic plasticity.
source: The capacity of SK channels to gate the induction of STDP during low-frequency single AP-EPSP pairing provides a means to negate the impact of accidental or spurious AP-EPSP pairings on synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings on STDP gating.

claim: The availability of SK channels is under the control of both metabotropic acetylcholine and glutamate receptors.
source: In addition, it provides a mechanism to regulate the extent of STDP induction given that the availability SK channels is under the control of both metabotropic acetylcholine and glutamate receptors (Buchanan et al., 2010; Giessel and Sabatini, 2010; Tigaret et al., 2016), as well as plasticity itself (Lin et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When APs are evoked shortly after EPSP onset, at the level of individual spines the depolarization associated with backpropagating APs will increase NMDAR activation and associated calcium influx.
source: When APs are evoked shortly after EPSP onset (e.g. +10 ms), while EPSPs at the soma will be shunted, as previously described (Häusser et al., 2001), at the level of individual spines the depolarization associated with backpropagating APs will increase NMDAR activation and associated calcium influx (Koester and Sakmann, 1998; Nevian and Sakmann, 2006; Schiller et al., 1998; Yuste and Denk, 1995), which would be expected to be regulated by SK channel channels, as occurs when APs are evoked before ESPs.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and inference from the current findings.

claim: Simulations using the model indicated that when APs were generated 10 ms after EPSP onset, turning SK channels off in the model increased NMDAR activation while having essentially no impact on AMPA current.
source: Consistent with this idea, simulations using our model indicated that when APs were generated 10 ms after EPSP onset turning SK channels off in the model increased NMDAR activation, while having essentially no impact on AMPA current (not shown).
evidence: This is a finding from computational modeling.

claim: Backpropagating APs have opposing effects on the currents generated during EPSPs.
source: In summary, we find that backpropagating APs have opposing effects on the currents generated during EPSPs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental and modeling findings.

claim: APs evoked just before EPSP onset reduce the electrochemical driving force for current flow through AMPA receptors, leading to EPSP suppression.
source: APs evoked just before EPSP onset reduce the electrochemical driving force for current flow through AMPA receptors, leading to EPSP suppression.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental and modeling findings.

claim: The depolarisation associated with backpropagating APs increases NMDAR activation, opposing the reduction in AMPA current.
source: At the same time, the depolarisation associated with backpropagating APs increases NMDAR activation, opposing the reduction in AMPA current.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental and modeling findings.

claim: Blocking dendritic SK channels increases NMDAR activation, reducing AP-induced EPSP suppression and leading to STDP induction.
source: As the extent of NMDAR activation is controlled by dendritic SK channels, blocking these channels increases NMDAR activation, reducing AP-induced EPSP suppression and leading to STDP induction.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental and modeling findings.
